title: Communicating With Families
answer: A school district once had a problem with truancy notices. The letters sent to families were written in legal language, warning of consequences and citing the education code.

papers.title: Lifting Up Attendance in Rural Districts: A Multi-Site Trial of a Personalized Messaging Campaign
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT in 47 rural districts, 16 states: absences down 1.7% to 4.5% at about $4 per student; 0.2 to 0.5 days saved.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence-assisted Translation and Interpretation for Communication With Patients Who Have Language Barriers: A Systematic Review
papers.venue: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine (abstract)
papers.finding: 18 studies: 62% flagged serious errors; accuracy lower for Haitian Creole and Vietnamese; use professional interpreters when possible.

papers.title: Can Personalized Attendance Information Mitigate Student Absenteeism? Evidence from Six Randomized Field Trials
papers.venue: Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: Six district-run RCTs, 78,000 PreK to 12 students: personalized parent messages cut absences 1.9%.

papers.title: Using Existing School Messaging Platforms to Inform Parents about Their Child's Attendance
papers.venue: Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT in four Atlanta-area districts using existing platforms at zero marginal cost: absences down 2 to 3%; neediest parents hardest to reach.

papers.title: Partnering with immigrant families to promote language justice and equity in education
papers.finding: Focus groups with Spanish, Portuguese, and Cantonese-speaking families: poor interpretation reduced access to special education services and trust in schools.

papers.title: Using Behavioral Insights to Improve School Administrative Communications: The Case of Truancy Notifications
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT, N = 131,312: plain-language, supportive truancy notices worked about 40% better than legalistic ones.

papers.title: Reducing Parent-School Information Gaps and Improving Education Outcomes
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT in low-income Chilean schools: weekly texts on attendance, grades, and behavior raised math by 0.09 SD.

papers.title: Your Child Missed Learning the Alphabet Today: A Randomized Trial of Sending Teacher-Written Postcards Home to Reduce Absences
papers.venue: Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT, 5,552 PreK to grade 2 students: postcards with a teacher note on missed content cut absences 8.3%.

papers.title: Leveraging Parents through Low-Cost Technology
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT, middle and high school: weekly automated texts on missed work, grades, and absences cut course failures 27% and raised class attendance 12%.

papers.title: Using behavioral insights to increase attendance at subsidized preschool programs: The Show Up to Grow Up intervention
papers.venue: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT in Chicago subsidized preschools: parent texts cut chronic absence 9.3 percentage points (20%).

papers.title: To Google Translate or not? Newcomer Latino communities in the middle
papers.finding: Vignettes show machine-translated school notices backfiring with Spanish-speaking families; proposes a readability checklist before translating.

papers.title: Reducing Student Absenteeism in the Early Grades by Targeting Parental Beliefs
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT in 10 districts, grades K to 5: parent mailings cut chronic absence 15%.

papers.title: Reducing student absences at scale by targeting parents' misbeliefs
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT, parents of 28,080 high-risk K-12 students: personalized mailings on total absences cut chronic absence by 10% or more by correcting parents' underestimates.

papers.title: Development of machine translation technology for assisting health communication: A systematic review
papers.caveat: Review quality depends on included studies.
papers.finding: 27 studies: machine translation works best on simple sentences and Western European languages; literature points to MT as a first draft followed by human correction.

children.name: Weekly Updates That Make a Difference
children.blurb: Weekly updates that make a difference are short, specific, frequent messages to families about missed assignments, grades, and absences, sent while there is still time to help.

children.name: Attendance Messages
children.blurb: Attendance messages are brief, personalized communications to families that state a child's actual number of absences or what the child missed in class.

children.name: Plain Language
children.blurb: Plain language means rewriting school policies, notices, and forms so families can understand and act on them.

children.name: Translation With Human Review
children.blurb: Translation with human review means using machine translation for everyday school messages while having a fluent person check anything critical before it goes to families.

children.name: Human Interpreters for Sensitive Meetings
children.blurb: Some school conversations are too consequential for machine translation.

children.name: Conferences and Positive Notes
children.blurb: Conferences and positive notes are two everyday ways teachers communicate with families, and AI can help draft both.

children.name: Website Helpers and Resource Directories
children.blurb: A website helper is a chat tool on a district website that answers common family questions about enrollment, schedules, and services at any hour, using only verified district information and saying clearly when it does not know.

children.name: Emergency Messages
children.blurb: Emergency messages are pre-written templates for situations such as a lockdown, a weather closure or a bus delay, drafted and translated with AI help and reviewed by people before anything happens.

children.name: Social Media and Media Consent
children.blurb: Social media and media consent means using AI to help draft school posts and design graphics while keeping a strict human check on student photos.

children.name: Engaging Families
children.blurb: Engaging families means using AI to help schools understand family feedback, explain AI to parents, and support home learning, while keeping people in charge of judgment.

children.name: Reaching Families Who Are Hardest to Reach
children.blurb: Reaching families who are hardest to reach means checking whether messages actually arrive and then using other contact methods when they do not.

children.name: Conversation, Not Just Announcements
children.blurb: This idea is two way translated messaging through TalkingPoints, so families can reply to teachers in their own language and get replies in theirs.

children.name: Protecting Family Privacy in Messages
children.blurb: Protecting family privacy in messages means keeping student details such as grades, absences and behavior inside messaging systems the district controls and covers with a signed data privacy agreement.

children.name: Five Questions Every Parent Should Ask
children.blurb: Five Questions Every Parent Should Ask is a family communication tool built on the idea that parents have a right to understand how their children's school uses AI.

sections.body: Communicating with families is the part of school life where districts send notices, updates, attendance messages, translations, conference invitations, emergency alerts, and other information that families need to understand and act on. The book says AI can draft messages in plain language, translate them into families' languages, and summarize long documents. It can also cause harm when translations mislead, chat tools fail, or messages go out without the care they deserve. The chapter treats this work as central because how schools communicate affects what families do, and small wording changes can have large effects. The book describes family communication research as one of the strongest areas in this Volume, with several randomized trials showing that messages that are clear, frequent, and personal lead to better attendance and grades.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The book finds that plain, supportive, and personal communication works, including attendance messages and weekly updates, and that translation needs human review. It reports that legalistic truancy notices did worse than plain ones, and that unchecked translation is the common failure pattern because a translated notice can say something different from the original. Poor translation damages trust, especially for families the district most needs to reach, and machine translation is most reliable for simple sentences and Western European languages, and the literature treats it as a first draft that a person corrects. The rule is that AI may produce a draft, but a person is responsible for every important word. The board question is whether families can understand district messages and act on them, with clear, timely messages in their own languages and human review for anything critical.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: Teachers and leaders can start with Weekly Updates That Make a Difference and Attendance Messages for routine contact and absence reduction, then use Plain Language, Translation With Human Review, and Human Interpreters for Sensitive Meetings to make messages clear and language access safe. Conferences and Positive Notes, Website Helpers and Resource Directories, Emergency Messages, and Social Media and Media Consent cover the different channels and consent rules a school must manage. Engaging Families, Reaching Families Who Are Hardest to Reach, Conversation, Not Just Announcements, and Protecting Family Privacy in Messages show how to build relationships, reach families who are hardest to reach, make communication two way, and keep family information private. Parents can go to Five Questions Every Parent Should Ask to know what to ask about a school's use of AI. Leaders can use the whole set to check whether messages are clear, timely, translated well, and reviewed by people when it matters.
